description: We are Cosmic Pathfinders, a team passionate about space, science, and technology. Our project, Forgotten Footprints, is an educational website that explores objects left behind after space missions, sharing their stories, locations, and scientific value. We value teamwork, research, creativity, and problem-solving. We welcome curious participants, especially those skilled in web development, graphic design, research, and writing.
summary:
Forgotten Footprints is a bilingual space museum and scientific archive documenting physical traces of human exploration beyond Earth, focusing on the Moon and Mars. It highlights spacecraft, instruments, and equipment left behind, recovered, or deployed.

The archive contains 22 sourced records (17 lunar and 5 Martian) and 35 timeline events. Each record presents an object's identity, mission, purpose, status, condition, location confidence.

Visitors can explore planetary galleries, search and filter artifacts, compare records, follow mission families, and inspect conceptual 3D models. Features include a timeline, discovery journal, glossary, quiz, myth-versus-fact cards, and a guided presentation route.

The platform supports English and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts, and adapts to mobile screens. Built with HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and custom WebGL, it runs from index.html without a server, installation, build step, external libraries, APIs, or internet connection.

Scientific accuracy is central. The archive distinguishes recovered hardware from objects still on another world and labels coordinates as verified, approximate, mission markers, or unplotted. 3D models and planetary scenes are illustrative, not engineering reconstructions or maps. The project is independent and does not claim NASA endorsement.

Forgotten Footprints makes overlooked space hardware accessible, preserving the historical value of exploration beyond Earth for curious learners too.
details:
Forgotten Footprints is a bilingual, interactive space museum and scientific archive documenting the physical traces of human exploration on the Moon and Mars. Visitors can explore 22 individually sourced artifact records, follow a timeline of mission events, and examine interactive 3D exhibits. The archive also includes search and filtering, artifact comparisons, and short learning activities.

The project looks at landers, rovers, instruments, and other mission hardware as part of the history of exploration. By making these objects easier to discover and understand, it aims to support public learning and encourage more thoughtful preservation of humanity’s presence beyond Earth.

We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using browser-native WebGL for the 3D scenes. Planet surfaces and artifact models are generated in the browser, and original SVG illustrations provide additional visuals. The core experience works offline and requires no installation. The site supports both English and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts.

The creative idea is to tell the story of exploration through what missions leave behind. Visitors can inspect an artifact’s parts and read about its purpose, present condition, and significance. To keep the archive reliable, we considered source quality, object identity, location uncertainty, and the limits of each model. The 3D exhibits are clearly presented as conceptual models, and records link to their sources.
